content.content:
To see the whole diagnostic, with its Java stack, run the program directly, from `ProjectFortress/` as the harness does, because an import is looked up in the current directory first:

    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress -debug stacktrace tests/X.fss

The direct run and the harness use different heaps (`interpreter.md`, "Running a program").

### Compiled tests

Compiled tests are the `.test` files in `compiler_tests/`, `library_tests/` and `other_compiler_tests/`. They link with the library's jars in the tree's `default_repository/caches`. If a build started the caches again, or the tree's caches are empty, run the library order first (`build-and-caches.md`).

The script is `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh`. `climb-batch-N` is the folder's real name, not a placeholder. Run your own tree's copy: it runs the tree that it is in.

    ONE_JVM=1 explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh <label> \
        ProjectFortress/compiler_tests X.test Y.test > <tree>/tmp/junit-<label>.txt 2>&1

- `<label>` is any word. It marks the run's lines in the output. The script writes to standard output only, so redirect it to your `tmp/`.
- With `ONE_JVM=1`, the whole list runs in one `fortress junit` run, in one JVM. The compile and link tests run before the run tests, as in the suite. Without `ONE_JVM=1`, each file gets its own JVM.
- It removes the named components' entries from the tree's `default_repository/caches` before the whole list and after it, not between files. So a link test and the run test that uses its jar pass in one call, with or without `ONE_JVM=1`.
- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing, as `harness-one.sh` does.
- It removes the Java stack frames, and cuts each line at 240 characters.
- Its JVMs keep their temporary files in the tree's `tmp/`, and run at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`.

To run the same list in one JVM without the script, and without its removal of cache entries:

    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress junit compiler_tests/X.test compiler_tests/Y.test

Run all the new files of one test folder together, in one JVM, as the suite does. A test that passes alone can fail beside others.

## One unit-test class, or one track

To run one unit-test class: `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=BitsJUTest`. It uses the tree's own caches and the shell's `FORTRESS_THREADS`.

To run tracks of testFast whole, run their target. Each target runs its tracks as testFast does, with the same JVMs and private caches:

- `ant testCompiler`: the compiler and othercompiler tracks.
- `ant testOtherCompiler`: the othercompiler track.
- `ant testLibrary`: the library track.
- `ant testQuick`: the three tracks.

## The checker and the one library

- F-?1 **The compiled checker reduces a formula once in each analyzer, answers an exclusion asked again with fresh inference variables from a memo, and finds a type by its name once per trait table.** Each memo's key holds every input its answer reads: a reduction is kept by its formula on the analyzer (`TypeAnalyzer.reduced`, `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala:589-609`); an exclusion by the question with its type inference variables renamed apart, from an empty cycle history only (`:408-439`, `:985-1015`), and shared through the trait table where it read no context (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/TraitTable.scala:150-156`); a type's lookup and its declaration search by the name (`TraitTable.scala:34-68`). An answer that read the context is marked, so a hit on it is a context read; a computation that opened a size is not kept. Each memo has a switch, default on: `fortress.analyzer.reduce.cache`, `fortress.analyzer.exclusion.cache`, `fortress.analyzer.typecons.cache`. The count stage took 437 s before and 97 s after in one loaded session (the skeptic's pair: 392 s and 83 s), its tables and whole outputs equal; audits that computed every reused answer again found 0 differences, 7.15M reductions, 153,930 exclusions and 156M lookups on the count stage and 428M reuses on the distance stage. A new memo of the checker follows the same rule. Gated by `ReductionMemoJUTest`, `ExclusionMemoJUTest` and `TraitTableMemoJUTest` (misc track) and by the count stage's table. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-solver-speed/REPORT.md` sections 1, 4, 6 and 7.
  from: compile-ladder/rung-solver-speed/REPORT.md, "1. What changed and why"; by: climb batch 16's gather; note: rung S's record, its first FACTS entry
- F-?2 **Every method of the build is within HotSpot's 8,000-byte limit but twelve, and a misc-track test fails when that changes.** `MethodSizeJUTest` reads every class of `ProjectFortress/build` with `java.lang.classfile`; it fails on an unlisted method past the limit and on a listed one gone from the build or back under it, and each entry of its list carries its size and what runs it. The twelve: `NodeReader.readNode`, the three parsers' `pCharLiteralContent$1`, `ExprDisambiguator.walk`, `Misc.checkExprMisc`, `HygienicRenamer.walk` (nothing constructs a `HygienicRenamer`), `MagicNumbers.<clinit>` and four `DirectedRoundingTestData` data methods that no suite runs. `WalkerJUTest` still guards `Walker` (F-231). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-solver-speed/REPORT.md` section 8.
  from: compile-ladder/rung-solver-speed/REPORT.md, "8. The guard's list"; by: climb batch 16's gather; note: rung S's record, its second FACTS entry
- F-231 **The generated AST walker is split into methods that the JVM compiles; as one method it ran interpreted and set the checker's time.** `Walker.walk`, which `ScalaAstGenerator` writes into `FortressAst.scala`, was one method of 31,704 bytes, past HotSpot's 8,000-byte limit, and the checker's substitutions and normalizations all go through it. Split in order into eight methods, with identical output, the count stage with row 680's repair takes about 340 s on an idle machine instead of 911 s, and the distance stage 931 s instead of 2,375 s. About 95 % of what remained was the solver reducing formulas again, which its memos now answer (F-?1); with the reduction memo alone the count stage's profile held the exclusion questions (`pExc`, `dExc`) at about 62 to 65 % of a run a third as long, and the final code has no profile. Gated by `WalkerJUTest`. Detail: `perf-probes/checker-speed-2/REPORT.md` sections 2 and 6; `compile-ladder/rung-solver-speed/REPORT.md` section 5.
  from: compile-ladder/rung-solver-speed/REPORT.md, "5. The profiles"; by: climb batch 16's gather; note: rung S's record, "Corrections of entries that are now wrong"

On rung S's final code the distance stage reads 48 without it ('DISTANCE DOWN   49 -> 48 (-1)'), while the audit copy of the same code, which computes every reused answer again, reads 49 with it and 0 differences in 428M reuses ('DISTANCE SAME   49'); `explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/compare.sh:16-18` reads a move of 2 to 4 errors as the checker's run-to-run variation, and this move is one error. Rung H found the cause: `ApiTypeExtractor` matches a component function's left-out return type by name only, over `DeclaredFunction`s that hash by identity, so `BIG LEXICO(g)` takes `BIG LEXICO()`'s `BigReduction` return type when that declaration comes first (row 737; `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/ApiTypeExtractor.scala:116-122`, `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/index/DeclaredFunction.java:25`); by "Type Inference for Components" it takes `TotalComparison` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:98`), so a match by parameter types would remove `:130` for good and lower the count and the distance by one. When, and in which checker rung, is that match scheduled? Default: the batch record's reading of the gate, 49, or 48 with `:130` gone (`coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-16.md:380`), and row 737 open, gated by `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXOmittedReturnTypeFromApi.test`. Evidence: `compile-ladder/rung-solver-speed/REPORT.md:286-296`, `compile-ladder/rung-solver-speed/SKEPTIC.md:238-240`, `compile-ladder/rung-ast-hashes/REPORT.md:167` (section 4.3) and `:309`.
- H.worker.2 and H.skeptic.2 of climb batch 16's rung H: with the nodes' hashes fixed, two count runs of one tree no longer differ in the api order or a union's members, whatever code asked for identity hashes first (the H runs at 1 and 1000 equal the change's run; the skeptic's `SkHashTypecase` prints one spelling under three JVM hash modes). Should P-148's comparison still count a line that differs only in order as equal, as the skill states it (`.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/compiler.md:130`)? A rung's edit now moves such an order only through what it changes, or through row 737. Default: the allowance stays as written. Evidence: `compile-ladder/rung-ast-hashes/REPORT.md:279`, `compile-ladder/rung-ast-hashes/SKEPTIC.md:109` and `:116`.

73:- F-80 **The compiled checker judges two functional methods of one name by the Meet Rule for Functional Methods, in each type that provides both, and keys its overloading memo on the check's inputs.** Such a type must provide their meet, compared without the self parameter. F-88 says what a type provides. Unchecked: a pair one of whose declarations is the component's own abstract one (row 572), and a pair that only an object expression provides (row 570). Gated by `compiler_tests/FunctionalMethodMeet*`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-overloading-checker/REPORT.md` section 5.
148:- F-145 **Walk refuses at load an object that leaves an inherited abstract method uncovered, an `override` that overrides nothing, and a generic type that breaks the Meet Rule for Functional Methods.** Bodies at narrower parameter types define an abstract method only where together they cover its parameter types, with `comprises` clauses read, as P-147 decides: each position is split through the clauses, and every combination of parts must lie inside one body. A search that does not settle refuses the object: a cycle, a symbolic or unreadable type, 10,000 steps or 4,096 combinations. A generic object is not checked (row 665), and an object whose one covering definition has a static parameter of its own is refused (row 728). The compiled checker covers the same way, within the same bounds, except where a method has static parameters of its own (row 725). F-147 gives the `override` check and F-142 the Meet Rule's. Gated by `tests/AbstractMethod*Walk` (`AbstractMethodCoverUnsettledWalk` among them), `OverrideNothing*Walk` and `compiler_tests/AbstractMethodCoveredPairs`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-coverage/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 6; `compile-ladder/rung-duplicates-coverage/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 8.
153:- F-228 **Under walk, a reduction or a comprehension that writes no static argument instantiates its big operator by the declared type of its value, else by the join of its elements' run-time types, else at its bound; so `__bigOperator`'s `body(i: I)` is typed.** It builds P-48 by the coordinator's call (the walk probe's way 6 + 7), and lifts D2. The declared type is a local variable's, or a top-level or local function's declared return type, also where the clause form ends a block; otherwise the clauses run once into the library's collector (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:1318-1437`), and the operator is instantiated at the elements' join. The hint is an argument to the operator's own instantiation, outside the per-argument caches (`EvaluatorBase.instantiateBigOperator`). Left open: an empty clause form no declared type directs (row 716), a comprehension no declared type reaches (rows 20 and 717), a user big operator whose declared result is its own trait (row 718), an argument of a call (rows 510 and 705). Gated by `tests/UnwrittenListMapComprehensionWalk`, `UnwrittenComprehension*Walk`, `ComprehensionTypedBindingWalk`, `UnwrittenSetBigOperatorsWalk`, `UnwrittenEmptyFloatSumWalk` and `IntMapComprehensionTypedWalk`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-elements/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 5.
182:- F-223 **The specification's No Duplicates Rule is the papers' non-strict rule, and the compiled checker applies it, to functional methods wherever their `self` parameters stand.** Two declarations of one name may not each be applicable to every call to which the other is, as in the type group's papers of 2011 and 2019 (P-26). The checker refuses such a pair, two functional methods at different `self` positions among them: "There are multiple declarations of f with the same parameter type", naming the domain of the declaration written first. It checks no symbolic operator (row 584) and reads no abstract functional method of a trait the component declares (row 727); such a pair passes it and stops the code generator (rows 726 and 727). Walk runs one of such a pair in two shapes (rows 373 and 549). Gated by `compiler_tests/XXXNoDuplicatesRule`, `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleSelfPositions` and `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleSelfPositionsPlain`, the checker's departures by `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleSelfPositionsOperator` and `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleAbstract`, and walk's departure by `tests/XXXNoDuplicatesRuleWalk`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-popl-examples/REPORT.md` section 4, its `SKEPTIC.md` section 2, and `compile-ladder/rung-duplicates-coverage/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 8.

The restatement follows the revival's decision of 23~September 2026 that the

reasoning is in

\item[Effect] Declarations of one name may differ in their static parameters,
as \library's do.
The compiled type checker refuses the pair of the Return Type Rule's example,
which it accepted before and whose compiled class then failed verification, and
an override whose return type reorders its static parameters, which it accepted
before and which then failed at run time (row~398).
Neither implementation runs every set these rules allow.
The compiled type checker refuses more than the Return Type Rule where the more
specific declaration's parameter type is an object type, as in
\EXP{\VAR{ident}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON{}T} beside
\EXP{\VAR{ident}(x\COLON \TYP{Circle})\COLON \TYP{Circle}} where \TYP{Circle} is an
object (row~542); the compiled code generator fails on two declarations with
static parameters whose bounds differ, the pair the Return Type Rule allows in
\secref{overloading-static-params} among them, and on the example of the type
group's paper of 2019 that overloads a method over an array list and a list
(row~537); and the interpreter refuses at load two declarations with static
parameters of which no pair of parameter types excludes each other (row~159),
that example among them (row~539).
Jan's example is still not a valid overloading, its two declarations having the
same parameter type.
The compiled type checker applies the No Duplicates Rule as it is now stated:
it refuses two declarations whose parameter types, read over their instances,
are each a subtype of the other, ``There are multiple declarations of \VAR{dup}
with the same parameter type'', two functional methods among them wherever their
\KWD{self} parameters stand.
It reads the abstract functional methods that a trait or object provides as it
reads the abstract dotted ones, so that an abstract functional method beside a
concrete one with the same parameter type is among the pairs it refuses, which
only its code generator refused before, as a malformed overload set.
It checks no overloading of an operator whose name is not a word of capitals
(row~584 of the revival's gap ledger): two declarations of such an operator with
the same parameter type pass it, and only its code generator refuses them, as a
malformed overload set (row~726).
The interpreter loads such a pair and runs one of them where both declarations
have static parameters and their parameter types mention one parameterized
type, as \VAR{dup}'s do (row~373), and where one has static parameters and the
other's parameter type is its bound (row~549).
The calculus of \appref{overloading-calculus} keeps its rule that two
declarations with the same number of parameters have static parameters with the
same bounds; it admits fewer overloadings than these chapters, so that its valid
programs are still valid, and its rules and its soundness claim are unchanged
(\secref{revival-calculi}).

declarations are applicable, so we ignore them for most of this chapter.

content.content:
The compiled type checker refuses more than the Return Type Rule where the more
specific declaration's parameter type is an object type, as in
\EXP{\VAR{ident}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON{}T} beside
\EXP{\VAR{ident}(x\COLON \TYP{Circle})\COLON \TYP{Circle}} where \TYP{Circle} is an
object (row~542); the compiled code generator fails on two declarations with
static parameters whose bounds differ, the pair the Return Type Rule allows in
\secref{overloading-static-params} among them, and on the example of the type
group's paper of 2019 that overloads a method over an array list and a list
(row~537); and the interpreter refuses at load two declarations with static
parameters of which no pair of parameter types excludes each other (row~159),
that example among them (row~539).
Jan's example is still not a valid overloading, its two declarations having the
same parameter type.
The compiled type checker applies the No Duplicates Rule as it is now stated:
it refuses two declarations whose parameter types, read over their instances,
are each a subtype of the other, ``There are multiple declarations of \VAR{dup}
with the same parameter type'', two functional methods among them wherever their
\KWD{self} parameters stand.
It reads the abstract functional methods that a trait or object provides as it
reads the abstract dotted ones, so that an abstract functional method beside a
concrete one with the same parameter type is among the pairs it refuses, which
only its code generator refused before, as a malformed overload set.
It checks no overloading of an operator whose name is not a word of capitals
(row~584 of the revival's gap ledger): two declarations of such an operator with
the same parameter type pass it, and only its code generator refuses them, as a
malformed overload set (row~726).
The interpreter loads such a pair and runs one of them where both declarations
have static parameters and their parameter types mention one parameterized
type, as \VAR{dup}'s do (row~373), and where one has static parameters and the
other's parameter type is its bound (row~549).
The calculus of \appref{overloading-calculus} keeps its rule that two
declarations with the same number of parameters have static parameters with the
same bounds; it admits fewer overloadings than these chapters, so that its valid
programs are still valid, and its rules and its soundness claim are unchanged
(\secref{revival-calculi}).

Walk reads two generic declarations each over its own instances, takes an if clause only as a Boolean or a Maybe, and reads a user big operator's result through its BigOperator supertype

Climb batch 16, rung W (wip/rung-walk-overload-if, b4b5e20aa..3f28cbfee), composed from the branch's net change with the skeptic's fix aa4b46d6e. - Rung W's five specification sentences were corrected after K's hunk, in changes.tex and inference.tex.
- Rows 740 and 741 are now named among the departures in the "Overloading with static parameters" Effect.

- F-53 and F-145.

- The gather tree /home/user/fortress-gather16.
